analysis.one_liner: Blocks federal fines and penalties against anyone who could not reasonably have known a rule existed or what it meant.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to a subcommittee that held one hearing in July 1998, and died when Congress adjourned in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred federal agencies and courts from punishing anyone for violating a federal regulation unless the rule had been published in the Code of Federal Regulations or the Federal Register, was actually known to the person, or would have been found by someone making a reasonable, good-faith search of the rules. It would also have barred penalties when a rule was too vague to give 'fair warning,' and would have wiped out penalties applied retroactively when an official had given misleading guidance that the person relied on. Its stated purpose is due process: no punishment without notice. In practice, the biggest beneficiaries would have been regulated businesses, which could contest fines by arguing they could not know or understand a rule.
analysis.who_benefits: Any person or business facing a federal fine or penalty for violating a regulation they claim they could not have known or understood. That shield is available to everyone, but the parties most likely to invoke it — and with the legal resources to litigate it — are regulated companies facing environmental, safety, or financial penalties. It also protects individuals and small firms from genuinely obscure or unpublished rules.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit any agency sanction for a rule violation if the agency finds the rule was not printed in the Code of Federal Regulations or the Federal Register, was not known to the person, or was not knowable through a reasonable, good-faith investigation of the applicable rules.

It would also bar penalties when a rule failed to give 'fair warning' — defined as a rule whose requirements a reasonable person acting in good faith could identify 'with ascertainable certainty' — and would bar retrospective sanctions where an official misled the person about what a rule required and the person reasonably relied on that guidance.

The bill's findings state that Americans have a due process right to learn what regulations mean before they can be sanctioned for violating them, and that this would encourage agencies to make requirements clearly known.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the cost when violators of health, safety, environmental, and consumer rules escape penalties by claiming they lacked notice, which weakens the deterrence behind those rules. Agencies would face more litigation over every enforcement action, since any sanctioned party could argue the rule was unclear or unknown.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through weaker rule enforcement

drawbacks.text: Because the ban triggers if any one condition is met, a violator could escape a penalty for a rule that was actually printed in the Federal Register but not yet codified in the Code of Federal Regulations, even where the industry had ample reason to know the requirement — a loophole that could undermine enforcement of environmental and safety rules the bill itself acknowledges 'advance many important goals.'

The 'fair warning' standard — requirements identifiable 'with ascertainable certainty' — is stricter than existing constitutional due process notice doctrine, so it could invalidate penalties under rules courts currently consider clear enough to enforce.

Every enforcement action could spawn fights over what a regulated party knew or should have investigated, raising the cost and delay of penalizing violations that harm workers, consumers, and the environment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The principle behind the bill — no punishment without fair notice — is a legitimate one, and it protects small players as well as large. But the drafting is broad: by letting any violator off the hook whenever a rule was uncodified, arguably vague, or unknown to them, it would hand well-resourced regulated companies a standing defense against fines, with the cost falling on the public in the form of weaker deterrence. A narrower version limited to genuinely unpublished or retroactive rules would have been less costly.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee referred the bill to its Commercial and Administrative Law Subcommittee, which held one hearing in July 1998; no markup or floor vote ever happened, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Representative George Gekas of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on June 11, 1998, with 14 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.
On June 18, 1998, the committee referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, which held a hearing on July 23, 1998.
No further action was taken; the bill never reached a committee vote or the House floor and expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's death left existing enforcement practices intact, so federal agencies retain the ability to fine violators without the new notice-based defenses, and regulated businesses gained nothing. To the extent the bill would have weakened enforcement, its failure favored the public; to the extent it would have protected people from obscure rules, they lost a potential safeguard.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal agencies; the bill's opponents by default

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan but minority support in the House.

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee, which held one hearing; the committee never marked it up or sent it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Of the bill's 17 cosponsors, 12 were Republicans and 5 were Democrats — bipartisan but leaning Republican, with no floor vote to reveal how the parties would have split.

industries.industry: Regulated businesses (manufacturing, energy, and other companies facing federal fines)
industries.note: The bill would give these firms a broad new defense against federal penalties: any fine could be challenged by arguing the rule was unpublished, unclear, or unknown despite a good-faith search. Larger companies with compliance departments and lawyers would be best positioned to use it, and the cost of weakened enforcement falls on workers, consumers, and the environment the rules protect.

Agencies would lose leverage in enforcement, since every sanction would face a statutory no-fair-warning defense, and they would face pressure to document and publicize every rule more aggressively. Some of that publicity burden could improve transparency for the public as well.
